Microbiology Lecture · LE 2 · Trans 4

RNA IV: Rabies, Slow Viruses, Oncogenic Viruses, HIV

Whole-Lesson Orientation

This lecture moves from an almost invariably fatal neurotropic infection to persistent neurologic disease, protein-only infectious agents, virus-associated carcinogenesis, and finally HIV as a complex lentiviral infection. The core study task is to connect viral structure with replication, then connect replication with pathogenesis, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment.

p. 1-20
Must Know Frameworkp. 1-20
Rabies: neuroinvasion after inoculation → CNS spread → centrifugal spread to tissues such as salivary glands.
Slow infections: long asymptomatic interval with progressive neurologic disease.
Prions: infectious misfolded proteins with no nucleic acid.
Tumor viruses: persistent infection plus altered growth control pathways can contribute to malignancy.
HIV: lifelong lentiviral infection with progressive CD4 T-cell depletion and persistent reservoirs.
High-Yield Orientation
TopicCore anchorLecture-level consequence

SSPEChronic nonpermissive measles infection of the CNSYears-long latency followed by progressive neurologic deterioration.
PMLJC virus reactivation in immunosuppressed patientsMultifocal demyelinating CNS disease.
PrionsPrPSc drives conversion of normal PrPCNo nucleic acid, no effective treatment, fatal transmissible spongiform encephalopathies.
Viral carcinogenesisActivation of oncogenic signaling plus loss of growth control, often with persistent infectionViruses are commonly cofactors rather than complete carcinogens.
HIVLentivirus that integrates as a provirus and forms genetic quasispeciesProgressive immune dysfunction, opportunistic infection, malignancy risk, and lifelong persistence.

Lecture Road Map

p. 1
  1. Rabies: properties → replication → pathogenesis → immune evasion → clinical disease → diagnosis → prophylaxis.
  2. Slow virus infections: SSPE and PML.
  3. Prions: structure, resistance, conversion of PrPC to PrPSc, CJD and kuru.
  4. Human cancer viruses: broad principles → retroviruses → DNA tumor viruses → specific oncogenic viruses.
  5. HIV: classification and structure → receptors and diversity → epidemiology → pathogenesis → clinical disease → diagnosis → treatment and prevention.

Rabies: Properties, Genome, and Replication

The lecture emphasizes that rabies is a rapidly progressive acute CNS infection caused by a Lyssavirus. The virus is highly neuroinvasive, but the detailed replication cycle begins with a classic non-segmented negative-strand RNA strategy.

p. 1-4

Core Properties of Rabies Virus

p. 1
  • Family: Rhabdoviridae. Genus: Lyssavirus.
  • Shape: rod or bullet shaped. About 75 × 180 nm in the properties section, with a later replication description of about 180 nm long and 80 nm wide.
  • Envelope: lipid bilayer with roughly 300-400 spike-like projections.
  • Genome: single-stranded RNA, non-segmented, negative-sense, about 12 kb. The lecture specifies 11,932 nucleotides.
  • Five encoded proteins: N, P, M, G, and L.
  • Required virion enzyme: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Negative-sense RNA cannot begin productive transcription without it.
  • Single serotype.

Reaction to Physical and Chemical Agents

p. 1
  • Survives storage at 4°C for weeks and at -70°C for years.
  • Inactivated by CO₂.
  • Killed rapidly by UV light or sunlight.
  • Killed by heat for 1 hour at 50°C.
  • Also killed by lipid solvents, trypsin, detergents, and extremes of pH.

What Each Rabies Protein Does

p. 2

G glycoprotein

Attachment and penetration. Binds host receptors. G trimers become clustered in the plasma membrane and participate in budding. The lecture also ties G to neuroinvasiveness and pathogenicity.

M protein

Structural bridge. Lies under the envelope, links envelope and ribonucleoprotein core, and later connects nucleocapsid with the intracellular tail of G trimers during assembly.

N protein

Genome encapsidation. The most abundant ribonucleoprotein protein. It tightly coats viral RNA. Accumulation of N is central to the switch from transcription to replication.

P protein

Polymerase cofactor. Binds L to the nucleocapsid and RNA. With L it forms the transcriptase or LP complex.

L protein

Large polymerase protein. Provides enzymatic activities required for RNA synthesis.

Genome Order and Intergenic Logic

p. 2

The lecture gives the genome order from the 3′ end as Leader or genomic promoter → N → P → M → G → L → Trailer at the 5′ end.

  • There are four intergenic regions between coding regions.
  • Intergenic nucleotides are not transcribed into viral mRNA.
  • Each junction contains an upstream gene-end sequence and downstream gene-start sequence.
  • This start-stop architecture forces orderly sequential transcription in the same order as the genome.

Primary Transcription

p. 2-3
  1. Attachment: viral G binds host receptors. The lecture notes efficient binding to neural cells and use of receptors on other cells such as muscle.
  2. Endocytosis and fusion: the virion enters an endosome. After fusion, internal components enter the cytoplasm.
  3. Uncoating: M dissociates from the nucleocapsid, exposing the ribonucleoprotein core.
  4. Transcription begins at the 3′ end: the first product is the Leader RNA. It has no cap or poly-A tail but carries an encapsidation signal used in replication.
  5. mRNA capping: each viral mRNA is capped at initiation.
  6. Polyadenylation and termination: at an intergenic region, the polymerase adds a poly-A tail and ends the upstream mRNA.
  7. Restart: the polymerase initiates and caps the next downstream mRNA.
Key Differentiator: Transcription Attenuationp. 3
70-80%: the transcriptase successfully resumes at the next gene junction.
20-30%: the transcriptase fails to resume and dissociates.
Result: progressively fewer polymerases reach downstream genes. N mRNA is most abundant. L mRNA is least abundant.
Why this matters: the virus makes more structural nucleocapsid protein and less of the enzymatic L protein.

Switch from Transcription to Genome Replication

p. 3

Early in infection, the LP complex primarily makes individual mRNAs. As N protein accumulates, the replication program changes.

N protein becomes abundantN mRNA is highest because of transcription attenuation.
↓
N binds the 5′ end of the nascent productBinding occurs at the encapsidation signal.
↓
Leader becomes encapsidatedEncapsidation tells the polymerase not to stop at intergenic junctions.
↓
Full-length positive-sense antigenome is madeThe antigenome is continuously synthesized and encapsidated.
↓
Trailer promoter drives a full-length negative-sense genomeThe resulting encapsidated RNA matches the original genomic sequence.
↓
New genomes support secondary transcription and assemblyNewly made L and P proteins can associate with progeny genomes.

Central principle: polymerase behavior depends on encapsidation of the nascent RNA. This is presented as a fundamental principle of non-segmented negative-strand RNA virus replication.

Assembly and Budding

p. 4
  • G protein is synthesized on rough ER-bound ribosomes and inserted into the ER membrane in type 1 orientation.
  • G is transported through the ER-Golgi pathway to the plasma membrane.
  • At the plasma membrane, G trimers form clusters or microdomains independently of M.
  • At the budding site, M interacts with the nucleocapsid and the cytoplasmic tail of G trimers.
  • Formation of this complex supports budding and release of infectious progeny virions.

Rabies: Pathogenesis, Clinical Disease, Diagnosis, and Prophylaxis

The lecture connects risk of disease to the site and intensity of inoculation, then follows the virus along peripheral nerves into the CNS and later out to tissues such as salivary glands.

p. 4-6

Animal Susceptibility and Antigenic Features

p. 4
  • Wide host range: infects all warm-blooded animals.
  • High susceptibility: foxes, wolves, coyotes.
  • Intermediate susceptibility: skunks, raccoons, bats.
  • Low susceptibility: opossums.
  • Virus may be distributed in CNS, saliva, urine, milk, and lymph nodes of infected animals.
  • G glycoprotein: associated with neuroinvasiveness and pathogenicity. Purified spikes generate neutralizing antibody.
  • Nucleocapsid antiserum: useful for diagnostic immunofluorescence.

Burden of Disease

p. 4
  • Worldwide lecture estimate: 59,000 deaths yearly.
  • Philippines: cases increased from 235 in 2020 to 426 in 2024.
  • The lecture states that all rabies cases resulted in death.
  • In 2024, 45% were from domestic pets and 56% from animals with uncertain vaccination.
  • Most cases were in adolescents and adults younger than 50 years.
  • More cases occur in countries with a low sociodemographic index.

Pathogenesis: From Bite to Saliva

p. 4
Infected saliva inoculatedUsually by bite or scratch from a rabid mammal.
↓
Local phase at the inoculation siteIncubation is usually 20-90 days. The virus remains at or near the site during incubation.
↓
Muscle interactionIn muscle, rabies binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at postsynaptic membranes of neuromuscular junctions.
↓
Centripetal neural spreadRetrograde fast axonal transport through peripheral nerves toward spinal cord or brainstem. Lecture rate is up to about 250 mm/day with about 12-hour delays at each synapse.
↓
CNS infectionRapid spread through neuroanatomic connections by fast axonal transport.
↓
Centrifugal spread to other tissuesAfter CNS infection is established, the virus reaches tissues including salivary glands and is secreted in saliva.

Risk increases with multiple bites and inoculation into highly innervated areas such as the face and hands.

Pathology: Negri Bodies

p. 4
  • Negri bodies are described as pathognomonic.
  • They are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions composed of rabies virus proteins.
  • They occur in Purkinje cells of the cerebellum and pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus.
  • They are not present in every case. The lecture gives an occurrence of about 80%.
  • The highest viral titers are found in the submaxillary salivary glands.

Normal Antiviral Signaling vs Rabies Immune Evasion

p. 4-5

Normal sequence: RIG-I detects viral RNA → IRF3 and IRF7 activation → IFN-β production → JAK-STAT signaling → ISG expression → antiviral effectors.

The lecture then assigns immune-evasion roles to several rabies proteins:

  • N protein: conceals viral RNA from RIG-I.
  • P protein: inhibits ISGs and IRF3/7, reducing IFN-β.
  • M protein: dampens innate immune gene expression.
  • G protein: reduces T-cell activation and promotes IL-10 secretion.

Net effect: poor cytokine and chemokine response, limited leukocyte entry into the CNS, absent neutralizing antibodies, and immune-cell apoptosis.

Prodrome and Two Major Clinical Forms

p. 5

Incubation: usually 1-3 months in the clinical section. Symptoms have been reported from 5 days after exposure to 8 years.

Prodrome: fever, malaise, headache, nausea, and vomiting. Early neurologic symptoms include paresthesia, pain, or pruritus near the exposure site.

Furious vs Paralytic Rabies
FeatureEncephalitic or furious rabiesParalytic rabies
Frequency~80%~20%
Dominant patternHyperexcitability and early brainstem involvementEarly prominent flaccid muscle weakness
Typical featuresFever, confusion, hallucinations, combativeness, seizures
Autonomic dysfunction including hypersalivation, gooseflesh, arrhythmia, priapism		Weakness often starts distally and progresses to quadriparesis and facial weakness
Sphincter involvement common
Sensory involvement mild
Classic distinctionHydrophobia and aerophobia
Periods of hyperexcitability alternate with lucidity		Hydrophobia and excitability are absent
Common confusionProgresses rapidly to coma and deathOften misdiagnosed as Guillain-Barré syndrome
CourseBrainstem dysfunction progresses rapidlyUsually survives a few days longer before multiple organ failure
Clinical Cuep. 5
Hydrophobia or aerophobia with early brainstem involvement strongly fits the lecture description of furious rabies.
Ascending or spreading flaccid weakness without hydrophobia can mimic Guillain-Barré syndrome and points toward paralytic rabies.

Diagnosis

p. 5
  • Immunofluorescence or immunoperoxidase staining: definitive pathologic diagnosis and evaluation for Negri bodies.
  • RT-PCR: amplifies portions of the rabies virus genome.
  • Serology: serum antibodies detected by immunofluorescence or neutralization tests.
  • Viral isolation: hamster and mouse cell lines may be inoculated, with identification by fluorescent antibody tests.
  • Animal observation: suspected rabid animals and animals showing encephalitis or unusual behavior undergo laboratory tissue examination.
Exam Trapp. 5
The lecture states that there are no tests that diagnose rabies before clinical symptoms appear.
This is why prevention and prompt post-exposure management are emphasized.

Pre-exposure Prophylaxis and Vaccine Response

p. 5-6
  • Immunologically naive PrEP: 2-site intradermal or 1-site intramuscular vaccine on day 0 and day 7.
  • Routine PrEP booster or serologic titers are considered when continued high risk of rabies exposure remains.
  • Vaccination generates a strong cellular immune response with CD4 helper cells and T cells.
  • Plasmablasts and memory cells appear early and correlate with rising antibodies.
  • A booster triggers a faster and stronger immune response.

Slow Virus Infections and Prions

Slow infections share a long clinically silent period followed by progressive neurologic disease. The lecture separates conventional viral causes from the unconventional prion diseases.

p. 6-7

Slow Virus Infections: Defining Pattern

p. 6
  • Chronic and persistent.
  • Long asymptomatic period lasting months or years.
  • Progressive neurologic disease.
  • Two broad groups in the lecture: conventional viral diseases and unconventional diseases caused by prions.

Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis

p. 6
  • Rare, chronic, progressive, demyelinating CNS disease.
  • Associated with a chronic nonpermissive measles infection. The virus remains in brain tissue but does not undergo full productive replication.
  • Frequency given in the lecture: about 1 in 100,000-500,000 measles cases.
  • Classical history: measles infection at an early age, around 2 years, then a 6-8 year latent interval.
  • Early clues: poor school performance, mood change, and personality change.
  • Progression includes intellectual deterioration, seizures, myoclonus or ataxia, and visual disturbance.
  • Late stage: unresponsiveness, quadriparesis, spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses.
  • CSF anti-measles antibody: invariably elevated. Oligoclonal anti-measles antibody is present.
  • Virus can be cultured from brain tissue. Viral antigen can be identified immunocytochemically. Viral genome can be detected by in situ hybridization or PCR.
  • No definitive therapy is available. Prevention is vaccination.

Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy

p. 7
  • Caused by JC virus, a member of Polyomaviridae.
  • Occurs in immunosuppressed patients and may follow therapeutic monoclonal antibody use such as in multiple sclerosis.
  • Mechanism: reactivation and replication of JC virus causes CNS demyelination.
  • Symptoms: visual deficits are most common. Mental impairment, weakness, ataxia, and seizures may occur.
  • MRI: multifocal asymmetric coalescing white-matter lesions in centrum semiovale, parieto-occipital region, and cerebellum.
  • Diagnosis: positive CSF PCR for JCV DNA plus the characteristic MRI lesion pattern. The lecture gives specificity of 92-100% with variable sensitivity.
  • No consistently effective therapy.
  • Mirtazapine may inhibit binding of JCV to its receptor on oligodendrocytes.

Prions: What Makes Them Different

p. 7
  • Proteinaceous infectious particles that lack nucleic acid.
  • Composed of alternatively folded proteins capable of self-propagation.
  • Described as epigenetically heritable.
  • Only known transmissible pathogens without RNA or DNA.
  • Can appear as infectious, genetic, or sporadic disorders.
  • Pathogenesis reflects accumulation of PrPSc, a misfolded form generated from normal PrPC.
  • Different prion strains can have different biologic properties.
Lecturer Emphasisp. 7
Normal PrPC is made in the endoplasmic reticulum, passes through the Golgi apparatus, and reaches the cell surface where it is anchored by a glycophosphatidylinositol anchor.

Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathy Properties

p. 7
  • Small: less than 100 nm.
  • No nucleic acid genome.
  • Extremely resistant to heat, disinfectants, and irradiation.
  • Can be inactivated by phenols, periodate, sodium hydroxide, or sodium hypochlorite.
  • Slow replication and prolonged incubation. Human incubation may be up to 35 years and often presents late in life.
  • Cannot be cultured in vitro.
  • Do not elicit a meaningful immune or inflammatory response.
  • No treatment and always fatal in the lecture.

Prion Pathogenesis

p. 7
Normal PrPᶜ reaches the cell surfaceIt is membrane-anchored by GPI.
↓
Abnormal PrPˢᶜ contacts normal PrPᶜConversion can occur at the surface or inside endocytic vesicles.
↓
Misfolding propagatesLipid raft microdomains and cofactors such as sulfated glycosaminoglycans or proteoglycans influence the process.
↓
PrPˢᶜ accumulatesAccumulation occurs in lysosomal membranes or extracellular amyloid plaques.
↓
Neural tissue degeneratesProgressive neurodegeneration produces the transmissible spongiform encephalopathy phenotype.

Kuru and Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease

p. 7
  • Kuru: historically spread by ritual cannibalism and described in the eastern highlands of New Guinea.
  • Classic CJD: progressive dementia, ataxia, and myoclonus. Death occurs in about 5-12 months.
  • Sporadic CJD: spontaneous conversion of normal prion protein. Lecture occurrence is about 1 case per million, usually over age 50.
  • Iatrogenic CJD: associated with contaminated surgical instruments or cadaveric human dura mater grafts.
Must Knowp. 7
Prions have no nucleic acid.
They provoke no inflammatory or immune response.
The lecture states that prion diseases have no treatment and are always fatal.

Human Cancer Viruses: General Principles and Carcinogenesis

The lecture presents tumor viruses as contributors to a multistep carcinogenic process. Persistent infection, viral gene products, host genetics, immune control, and additional mutations determine whether infection progresses to cancer.

p. 7-9

General Features of Viral Carcinogenesis

p. 7-8
  • Viruses are etiologic factors in several human tumors, including cervical cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma.
  • The lecture estimates that 15-20% of all human tumors have a viral cause.
  • Named viral associations include HPV, EBV, HHV-8, hepatitis B and C viruses, HIV, and HTLV.
  • Viral infections are much more common than virus-related tumors because viruses are rarely complete carcinogens.
  • Many tumor viruses establish persistent infection with a long latent period before malignancy appears.
  • Host genetic and immune factors are critical determinants of progression.
  • Different viral strains can differ in oncogenic potential.
  • Viruses may act directly by altering host growth control or indirectly through chronic inflammation and tissue injury.
  • Viral markers are usually detectable in tumor cells.
  • A single virus can be linked to more than one tumor type.

DNA vs RNA Tumor Viruses

p. 8
Major tumor-virus strategies
FeatureDNA tumor virusesRNA tumor viruses
Representative groupsPapilloma, polyoma, adeno, herpes, hepadna, pox groupsMostly retroviruses
Key transforming strategyEncode viral oncoproteins that are needed for viral replication and also perturb cell-growth controlReverse transcriptase makes a DNA copy that integrates as a provirus
Oncogene relationshipViral transforming genes do not have normal cellular counterparts in the lecture frameworkSome highly oncogenic retroviruses carry a transduced cellular oncogene
TempoDepends on persistent infection and additional cellular eventsHighly oncogenic viruses can transform rapidly. Weakly oncogenic viruses can require years

Carcinogenesis Is Multistep

p. 8
  • A normal cell becomes malignant only after multiple genetic changes.
  • Intermediate states include cells described as immortalized, hyperplastic, and preneoplastic.
  • Tumors usually develop slowly through cellular instability.
  • Mutations accumulate. Cells that acquire a growth advantage expand through selection.
  • Two central molecular themes are activation of oncogenes and inactivation of tumor suppressor genes.
  • A tumor virus usually acts as a cofactor. The lecture repeatedly frames viruses as necessary in some tumors but often not sufficient by themselves.

Viral Infection Cycle vs Cancer Development

p. 8

The lecture lists the ordinary infection sequence as attachment → entry and uncoating → replication and transcription → protein synthesis → assembly → release. This infection cycle is not itself cancer.

The important cancer connection is persistence. Long-term viral presence increases opportunities for genetic instability and malignant transformation.

Examples named in the lecture include hepatocellular carcinoma, gastric cancer linked with EBV and Helicobacter coinfection, cervical cancer, esopharyngeal carcinoma, Kaposi sarcoma, lymphomas, and adult T-cell leukemia or lymphoma.

Proto-oncogenes and Cellular Oncogenes

p. 9
  • Proto-oncogenes normally regulate cell growth, division, and differentiation.
  • Mutation or overexpression can convert them into oncogenes that drive uncontrolled proliferation.
  • Genetic damage or viral promoter insertion can activate proto-oncogenes.
  • A retroviral promoter can enhance expression of a neighboring cellular gene.
  • Incorrect or excessive expression disrupts normal regulation of proliferation, differentiation, and genome integrity.

Tumor Suppressor Genes

p. 9
  • Tumor suppressor genes act as negative regulators of cell growth.
  • The lecture emphasizes that both alleles generally must be inactivated for tumor formation.
  • RB: loss of function removes a brake on entry into S phase.
  • p53: normally halts the cell cycle or induces apoptosis when DNA is damaged.
  • The lecture states that p53 is mutated in about 50% of human cancers.
  • Loss of tumor-suppressor function permits unchecked division and accumulation of additional mutations.
High-Yield Recapp. 9
Activation of proto-oncogenes → uncontrolled growth.
Loss of RB or p53 → loss of cell-cycle and apoptosis control.
Viral oncogenesis often works by pushing one or both sides of this balance.

Tumor Viruses and the Host

p. 9
  • Persistent infection provides time for rare cellular events and transformation.
  • The immune system normally controls virus-infected cells.
  • When the host is immunosuppressed, transformed cells can grow with less immune restraint.
  • Examples in the lecture: organ-transplant recipients and people with HIV have higher risk of EBV-associated lymphomas and HPV-related cancers.
  • The balance between viral persistence and immune control strongly influences whether infection remains clinically silent or progresses to cancer.

Retroviruses and HTLV

Retroviruses are RNA viruses that use reverse transcriptase to make a DNA copy, then integrate that DNA into the host genome as a provirus. This persistent proviral state explains both their biology and their oncogenic potential.

p. 9-11

Retrovirus Properties

p. 9
Important properties of retroviruses
PropertyLecture detail
VirionSpherical. About 80-110 nm. Helical nucleoprotein within an icosahedral capsid.
CompositionRNA about 2%. Protein about 60%. Lipid about 35%. Carbohydrate about 3%.
GenomeSingle-stranded RNA. Linear. Positive-sense. 7-11 kb. Diploid. May be defective or carry an oncogene.
EnzymeReverse transcriptase inside the virion.
EnvelopePresent.
ReplicationReverse transcriptase makes DNA from genomic RNA. DNA integrates into the chromosome as a provirus. The provirus becomes the template for viral RNA.
MaturationVirions bud from the plasma membrane.
Biologic featuresMost infections do not kill cells. Cellular oncogenes can be transduced or cell genes can be activated. Provirus remains permanently associated with the cell and may be silent.

Morphologic Classes

p. 9
  • Type A: intracellular and non-infectious.
  • Type B: eccentric nucleoid.
  • Type C: largest group. Nucleoid is centrally located.
  • Type D: poorly characterized. Eccentric nucleoid with short spikes.

Retrovirus Classification

p. 10
  • Alpha retroviruses: avian leukosis and sarcoma viruses.
  • Beta retroviruses: mouse mammary tumor virus.
  • Gamma retroviruses: mammalian leukemia and sarcoma viruses.
  • Delta retroviruses: HTLV and bovine leukemia virus.
  • Epsilon retroviruses: fish viruses.
  • Spuma viruses: foamy-cell changes with no known disease.
  • Lentiviruses: slow chronic infections. HIV is the major example.

Exogenous vs Endogenous Retroviruses

p. 10
Exogenous and endogenous retroviruses
FeatureExogenousEndogenous
TransmissionActively transmitted from host to hostInherited as a permanent part of the host genome
Where viral gene sequences are foundOnly in infected cellsPresent in host DNA, including germline when inherited
BehaviorClassic infectious agent. Infection may lead to cell transformationUsually silent under host control. Can be activated under certain conditions
Human disease examples in lectureAll retroviruses known to cause disease in humans and animals, including HIV and HTLVInherited proviral genomes derived from ancient RNA tumor virus infection

Host Range and Receptors

p. 10
  • Cellular susceptibility depends heavily on the presence of a specific cell-surface receptor.
  • Ecotropic viruses: highly species specific. Replicate only in cells from the natural host.
  • Amphotropic viruses: broad host range because the receptor is widely distributed.
  • Xenotropic viruses: cannot replicate in cultured cells from their natural host but can infect cells from certain foreign species.

Retroviral Genetic Content

p. 10
  • The genome is diploid, with two RNA copies per virion. The lecture notes that this supports genetic backup and recombination.
  • Basic leukemia-virus genes are GAG, PRO, POL, ENV.
  • GAG: core proteins.
  • PRO: protease.
  • POL: reverse transcriptase.
  • ENV: envelope glycoprotein.
  • Delta retroviruses and lentiviruses contain additional regulatory genes downstream from ENV, such as TAX or TAT.

General Retrovirus Lifecycle

p. 10-11
Envelope binds receptor and coreceptorHIV-1 example: CD4 plus CCR5 or CXCR4.
↓
Fusion and core entryCapsid is released into the cytoplasm and traffics toward nuclear pores.
↓
Reverse transcriptionAt or near the nuclear envelope, uncoating and reverse transcription generate double-stranded DNA.
↓
IntegrationIntegrase inserts viral DNA into the host genome. The integrated DNA is the provirus.
↓
Host-cell expressionHost machinery transcribes viral genomic RNA and mRNAs. Viral proteins are translated. ENV enters the ER membrane.
↓
Assembly at plasma membraneViral RNA and proteins are directed to the membrane.
↓
BuddingImmature particles leave the host cell.
↓
Protease-mediated maturationCleavage of GAG permits formation of the fully infectious virion.
Key Differentiatorp. 11
Most retroviruses are not cytolytic.
Lentiviruses are the exception highlighted in the lecture and may be cytolytic.
The provirus remains integrated for the life of the infected cell.

Human T-Lymphotropic Virus

p. 11
  • HTLV has existed in humans for thousands of years.
  • Causative agent of adult T-cell leukemia or lymphoma.
  • Has marked affinity for mature T cells.
  • Does not carry a classic oncogene.
  • Viral expression is usually low in infected individuals.
  • LTR promoter and enhancer sequences respond to signals of T-cell activation and proliferation, allowing viral replication to track host-cell replication.
  • TAX is a trans-regulatory gene that alters viral and cellular gene expression. It supports replication and may contribute to cancer by disrupting growth control.
  • Lecture global estimate: about 20 million infected.
  • Transmission is mainly cell associated: breastfeeding, blood transfusion, shared needles, and sexual contact.
  • Early-life infection carries the greatest later risk of adult T-cell leukemia or lymphoma.

HIV vs HTLV in Tumor Biology

p. 11

HIV is cytolytic and non-transforming. It causes AIDS rather than directly converting normal cells into cancer cells.

HIV-associated cancers are therefore described as indirect consequences of immunosuppression. The lecture lists cervical cancer, Kaposi sarcoma, lymphomas, head and neck cancers, liver cancer, and oral cavity cancer.

DNA Tumor Viruses and Specific Oncogenic Viruses

DNA tumor viruses use viral proteins that directly alter host growth-control machinery. The lecture highlights interactions with p53, Rb, PP2A, PDGF-β receptor, and cellular signaling complexes.

p. 11-14

DNA Tumor Virus Oncoprotein Strategy

p. 11
  • Transforming genes are generally essential for viral replication.
  • These viral transforming genes do not have normal cellular counterparts in the lecture framework.
  • Their proteins bind normal host proteins and alter host function.
  • This differs from RNA tumor viruses, which may carry transduced cellular oncogenes or promote cancer through indirect mechanisms.

High-Yield Oncoprotein Interactions

p. 11-12
Viral oncoproteins emphasized in the lecture
VirusViral proteinHost target or effect
SV40 polyomavirusLarge T antigenBinds p53 and Rb, disabling major tumor-suppressor functions.

HPVE6Binds and degrades p53. Also disrupts DLG, MAGI-1, and MUPP-1.

AdenovirusE1B-55kBinds p53.

Hepatitis B Virus and Hepatocellular Carcinoma

p. 12
  • Hepadnaviridae. Enveloped, 42-nm spherical virus with a circular double-stranded DNA genome.
  • Major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma.
  • Most adult infections resolve. In neonates and young children, the lecture states that up to 90% may become chronic.
  • Chronic infection produces necrosis, inflammation, repeated liver regeneration, and cirrhosis, creating a background for HCC.
  • HBV X protein acts as a viral oncoprotein.
  • Aflatoxin can synergize with HBV to increase HCC risk.
  • Lecture estimate: 250 million people chronically infected and about 800,000 deaths per year from complications including cirrhosis and liver cancer.
  • HBV vaccination prevents infection and significantly reduces HCC risk.

Hepatitis C and Hepatocellular Carcinoma

p. 9
  • HCV is a member of Flaviviridae with a single-stranded RNA genome.
  • Chronic infection promotes long-term inflammation and cirrhosis.
  • It is therefore a major causal factor for hepatocellular carcinoma.
  • The lecture gives about 70 million chronic carriers, with roughly 1-5% developing HCC.
  • The cancer risk is presented as a combined effect of viral and host mechanisms rather than a single transforming oncogene.

Polyomaviruses: Structure and Replication

p. 12
Important properties of polyomaviruses
PropertyLecture detail
VirionIcosahedral, about 45 nm.
GenomeCircular double-stranded DNA, about 5 kbp.
EnvelopeNone.
Replication siteNucleus.
Key transforming proteinsEarly-region T antigens.
Key biologic pointViral oncoproteins interact with cellular tumor suppressor proteins and can drive host-cell DNA synthesis.

Polyomavirus Early vs Late Regions

p. 12
  • Early region: expressed soon after infection and encodes T antigens.
  • SV40 expresses large T and small T. Murine polyomavirus expresses small, middle, and large T antigens.
  • T antigens drive viral DNA replication and directly participate in transformation. Continuous expression is needed to maintain the transformed state.
  • Late region: encodes structural coat proteins used for virion assembly. Late proteins are not required for transformation and may not be expressed in transformed cells.
  • SV40 large T binding to p53 and Rb promotes S-phase entry, loss of growth inhibition, impaired apoptosis, and mutation accumulation.

Polyomavirus Clinical Associations

p. 12
  • About 70-80% of adults have antibodies, suggesting childhood infection is common.
  • Virus can persist in kidneys and lymphoid tissue.
  • Reactivation is linked to transplantation, pregnancy, HIV or AIDS, and immunosuppressive therapy.
  • BK virus: hemorrhagic cystitis after bone marrow transplantation and polyomavirus nephropathy after kidney transplantation. The lecture gives about 5% of transplant patients and notes potential graft failure.
  • JC virus: PML in immunocompromised patients. The lecture notes about 5% of AIDS patients developing PML.
  • Merkel cell polyomavirus: strongly linked to Merkel cell carcinoma. In many tumors the viral DNA is clonally integrated and viral oncogenes are required for tumor growth.

Papillomavirus Properties and Tropism

p. 13
Important properties of papillomaviruses
PropertyLecture detail
VirionIcosahedral, about 55 nm.
GenomeCircular double-stranded DNA, about 8 kbp.
EnvelopeNone.
ReplicationNucleus.
TropismHighly specific for epithelial cells of skin and mucous membranes.
Cancer linkMajor cause of human cancer, especially cervical cancer. E6 and E7 target p53 and Rb.

HPV Replication and Persistence

p. 13
AttachmentHPV first docks on extracellular matrix or basement membrane through heparan sulfate proteoglycans.
↓
EntryVirus enters mainly through endocytosis and uses the actin network for intracellular movement.
↓
Early endosomeCD63 and RAB5 help retain the particle. Acidic conditions begin uncoating. Viral DNA remains associated with L2.
↓
Endosomal escape and Golgi traffickingSecretase cleavage exposes L2 regions. Retromer and RAB proteins guide the DNA-L2 complex to the trans-Golgi network. L1 capsid proteins go to lysosomes.
↓
Nuclear transportDNA-L2 moves on microtubules and enters the mitotic nucleus during cell division. It localizes to PML nuclear bodies.
↓
PersistenceEarly proteins such as E2 tether viral DNA to host chromosomes during mitosis, supporting maintenance as host cells divide.

HPV Replication Across the Epithelium

p. 13
  • Viral nucleic acid resides in basal stem cells.
  • Early replication occurs in dividing basal cells.
  • Late genes encoding capsid proteins are expressed only in upper, fully differentiated keratinocytes.
  • Complete particles assemble in mature cells near the epithelial surface.
  • This dependence on host-cell differentiation makes papillomaviruses difficult to culture in ordinary cell systems.

HPV Types, Persistence, and Cancer Risk

p. 13-14
  • Benign warts: HPV 1, 2, 4, 7.
  • Epidermodysplasia verruciformis: HPV 5 and 8. May progress to cancer.
  • Low-risk mucosal types: HPV 6 and 11. Associated with genital warts and laryngeal papillomas.
  • High-risk types: HPV 16 and 18 have the strongest cervical-cancer association. Types 31, 33, 45, and 56 are listed as moderate risk.
  • In benign and premalignant lesions, HPV DNA is generally episomal.
  • In cancers, viral DNA can be integrated. The critical clinical step is persistent high-risk HPV infection.
  • Progression to cervical cancer occurs over years to decades.
  • Cell-mediated immunity is important for clearance. Most infections become undetectable within 2-3 years.

HPV Epidemiology, Screening, and Vaccination

p. 14
  • The lecture calls HPV the most common viral infection of the reproductive tract and gives an estimate of about 660 million infected worldwide.
  • Peak infection occurs in adolescents and young adults younger than 25 years.
  • HPV is linked to >99% of cervical cancers and >80% of anal cancers.
  • HPV 16 and 18 account for >70% of cervical cancers, with type 16 the most common.
  • HPV 6 and 11 cause about 90% of anogenital warts.
  • Pap smear screening greatly reduced cervical-cancer mortality by detecting precancerous changes.
  • HPV testing by DNA hybridization or PCR increases detection of high-risk types.
  • Bivalent vaccine: 16, 18.
  • Quadrivalent vaccine: 6, 11, 16, 18.
  • 9-valent vaccine: 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58.
  • Vaccination is preventive, not therapeutic. It does not treat established HPV disease.
  • The lecture states vaccine-induced immunity lasts at least 10 years based on current evidence.

Herpesviruses and EBV Oncogenesis

p. 14
  • Herpesviruses are large, enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses with an icosahedral capsid.
  • Typical pattern: acute infection → latency → lifelong recurrence.
  • EBV infects B lymphocytes and causes infectious mononucleosis. It can immortalize B lymphocytes in culture.
  • Malignancies listed in the lecture include Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin disease, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders.
  • LMP1 acts like a constitutively active growth-factor receptor and is central to B-cell transformation.
  • EBV nuclear antigens support immortalization. EBNA1 is the protein consistently expressed in Burkitt lymphoma cells and also helps infected cells evade cytotoxic T-cell recognition by impairing antigen processing.
  • KSHV or HHV-8 is linked to Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, and multicentric Castleman disease.

HIV: Classification, Structure, Genes, and Genetic Diversity

HIV is the lecture's most important lentivirus. Its defining biologic features are an integrated provirus, a complex retroviral genome, extensive envelope variability, and a cytocidal effect on key immune cells.

p. 14-16

Introduction and Classification

p. 14-15
  • HIV is a lentivirus and the cause of AIDS.
  • AIDS was first recognized in 1981. HIV-1 was isolated in 1983.
  • Without treatment, HIV infection is lifelong and most patients eventually develop fatal opportunistic disease.
  • HAART transformed HIV from a fatal disease into a manageable chronic condition.
  • HIV-1: responsible for the global pandemic. Groups M, N, and O are listed. Group M contains multiple subtypes and recombinant forms.
  • HIV-2: concentrated mainly in West Africa and divided in the lecture into 8 subtypes, A-H.
  • Both trace to simian immunodeficiency viruses. HIV-1 is linked to chimpanzees. HIV-2 is linked to sooty mangabeys.
  • gag and pol are highly conserved. Envelope proteins are much more variable, complicating vaccine development.

Properties of Lentiviruses

p. 15
Important properties of lentiviruses
PropertyLecture detail
VirionSpherical, about 80-100 nm, with a distinctive cylindrical core.
GenomeSingle-stranded RNA and diploid. Slightly larger and more complex than simple oncogenic retroviruses.
ProteinsEnvelope glycoproteins vary constantly. Reverse transcriptase and protease are essential for replication and infectivity.
ReplicationReverse transcriptase makes DNA. DNA integrates permanently as a provirus. Viral proteins are then expressed and particles mature.
Unique traitNot directly oncogenic. Lentiviruses are cytocidal and can kill the immune cells they infect, supporting chronic progressive disease that can culminate in AIDS.

HIV Structure and Core Genes

p. 15
  • A mature HIV virion has a characteristic bar-shaped or cylindrical nucleoid.
  • Like other retroviruses, HIV carries the core genes gag, pro, pol, and env.
  • Unlike simple retroviruses, HIV also has up to six accessory genes that contribute strongly to pathogenesis.

HIV Accessory Genes

p. 15
Accessory genes of HIV
GeneLecture role
TatIncreases transcription of viral genes and makes replication highly efficient.
RevExports unspliced RNA from the nucleus for late structural-protein production.
NefIncreases infectivity and weakens host defense by downregulating CD4 and MHC I.
VprSupports nuclear transport of viral genetic material and causes G2 arrest, favoring replication.
VpuIncreases CD4 degradation.
VifBlocks APOBEC3G, an antiviral factor.

Genetic Diversity and the env Gene

p. 15-16
  • Within a single patient, HIV exists as a quasispecies, a swarm of closely related viral genomes.
  • The diversity results from a high replication rate plus the high error rate of reverse transcriptase.
  • env encodes the viral envelope proteins.
  • gp120: surface subunit. Binds CD4 and coreceptors. Contains major neutralizing-antibody antigenic sites. It has 5 variable regions, with V3 emphasized as important for neutralization.
  • gp41: transmembrane subunit. Anchors the envelope glycoprotein and provides the fusion domain for viral entry.
Study Aidp. 16
gp120 = binding.
gp41 = fusion.
This is a compact study cue derived directly from the lecture-described roles.

HIV: Receptors, Natural Disease Pattern, and Epidemiology

The lecture links HIV's persistent disease pattern to receptor tropism, infection of macrophages and lymphocytes, continuous variation, and ongoing transmission through body fluids.

p. 16-17

Natural Disease Pattern

p. 16
  • Transmission occurs mainly through exchange of body fluids.
  • Once acquired, HIV persists for life, even when present at very low levels.
  • The high mutation rate generates quasispecies that adapt to changing conditions and evade host defense.
  • Lentiviruses progress through slow, defined stages.
  • Macrophages and monocytes are central. Lentiviruses can infect non-dividing or terminally differentiated cells, although productive replication begins when those cells are activated.
  • The lecture states that only about 1 in 1,000,000 monocytes may be infected, yet those cells can carry virus around the body. Dr. Obligar describes them as Trojan horses.
  • Lymphocyte-tropic strains are highly productive. Macrophage-tropic strains replicate more restrictively.

Host Factors Influencing Progression

p. 16
  • Age: young hosts are at higher risk.
  • Stress: may trigger disease.
  • Genetics: susceptibility varies.
  • Concurrent infections: can worsen progression, accelerate disease, or increase transmission risk.

HIV Receptors and Coreceptors

p. 16
  • HIV requires two receptor interactions.
  • First, gp120 binds CD4 on T lymphocytes and macrophages.
  • Second, the virus engages a chemokine coreceptor. This activates gp41 and triggers membrane fusion.
  • CCR5: major coreceptor for macrophage-tropic strains.
  • CXCR4: major coreceptor for lymphocyte-tropic strains.
  • Receptor molecules are also found in tissues including colon, cervix, and neurons.
  • Individuals with CCR5 mutations may be naturally resistant or have delayed progression.
  • α4β7 integrin helps HIV infection in the gut.
  • DC-SIGN on dendritic cells does not directly mediate entry but transports HIV to lymphoid tissues and enhances T-cell infection.

Global HIV Burden

p. 16-17
40.8 millionpeople living with HIV by end of 2024
1.4 millionchildren younger than 15 living with HIV
39.4 millionadults 15 years and older living with HIV
1.3 millionnew infections in 2024
630,000HIV-related deaths in 2024
>44 milliondeaths since the start of the epidemic
  • New infections declined about 40% from 2010 to 2024.
  • HIV-related deaths declined about 54% from 2010 and about 70% from the 2004 peak.
  • The lecture states that about 90% of new infections yearly occur in developing countries, with predominantly heterosexual transmission.

Philippines HIV Data in the Lecture

p. 17
  • Based on 2022 data, the lecture describes the Philippines as having the fastest-growing HIV epidemic in the Western Pacific region.
  • 418% change in new HIV infections since 2010.
  • 538% change in AIDS-related deaths since 2010.
  • As of March 2024, DOH reported an average of 55 new diagnoses per day.
  • Of 122,255 people living with HIV, 64% or 78,633 were taking antiretroviral therapy.
  • The lecture projects an estimated 189,000 PLHIV increasing to about 401,700 by 2030.

Routes of Transmission and Quantified Risks

p. 17
HIV transmission routes
RouteLecture details
Sexual contactBlood and semen can carry high viral loads. Genital-oral sex is included. Multiple partners and other STDs such as HSV-2, syphilis, and gonorrhea can increase risk up to 100-fold by increasing inflammation and mucosal injury. Asymptomatic persons can transmit.
Parenteral exposureHistorically, contaminated blood products infected more than 90% of hemophiliacs who received contaminated clotting factors. Shared needles remain a risk. Modern donor screening reduces transfusion risk to <1 in 1,000,000.
Mother-to-childTransmission can occur in utero, during delivery, or with breastfeeding. Without treatment, 13-40% of infants born to HIV-positive mothers become infected. Higher maternal viral load increases risk.
OccupationalNeedlestick transmission risk is <0.3%. Mucous-membrane risk is 0.09%. Lecture comparison: HCV about 1.8% and HBV about 6-30%.

HIV: Pathogenesis, Latency, Clinical Progression, and Complications

Untreated HIV is not truly dormant during the clinically silent period. The lecture repeatedly stresses intense ongoing viral replication, continuous mutation, progressive CD4 T-cell loss, and establishment of cellular reservoirs.

p. 17-19

Course of Untreated HIV

p. 17-19
Primary infectionAbout 4-11 days from mucosal infection to initial viremia.
↓
Viremia and disseminationViremia lasts about 8-12 weeks and seeds lymphoid organs.
↓
Acute HIV syndromeAt about 3-6 weeks, 50-75% develop a mononucleosis-like illness with a sharp fall in circulating CD4 cells.
↓
Initial immune controlWithin 1-3 months, viremia decreases and CD4 count partly rebounds. Virus is not eliminated and remains in lymph nodes.
↓
Clinical latencyOften around 10 years. Virus continues active replication at low clinically apparent levels.
↓
Progressive diseaseViral expression and plasma load rise. Constitutional symptoms, opportunistic infections, and neoplasms appear.
↓
AIDS and death without treatmentThe lecture states death usually follows within about 2 years of symptom onset or development of AIDS.
Must Knowp. 18
Clinical latency does not mean virologic latency.
The lecture states that around 10 billion HIV particles are produced and destroyed daily during this period.
Infected CD4 T lymphocytes have a half-life of about 1.6 days.

Viral Evolution During Progression

p. 18
  • Most HIV infections are initially founded by a single viral variant, so the earliest viral population is relatively homogeneous.
  • Rapid replication plus error-prone reverse transcriptase generates a growing pool of quasispecies.
  • With progression, plasma viral load rises and late-stage strains become more virulent and cytopathic.
  • The lecture describes a shift from M-tropic strains toward T-tropic strains as patients approach full-blown AIDS.

CD4 T Cells, Memory Cells, and Latent Reservoirs

p. 18
  • The cardinal immunologic feature is depletion of CD4 T lymphocytes.
  • Infected T cells can die directly from viral replication. Uninfected T cells can also be lost through indirect mechanisms.
  • CD4 cells normally activate macrophages, cytotoxic T cells, NK cells, and B cells. Their loss therefore disrupts multiple arms of immunity.
  • At a given moment, only a small fraction of CD4 cells are productively infected.
  • Some infected T cells survive and return to a resting memory state.
  • These resting memory cells may show little or no viral gene expression, yet retain the integrated provirus as a stable long-term reservoir.
  • Even on ART, the lecture states that fewer than 1 per 1,000,000 CD4 T cells may carry provirus.
  • The reservoir declines extremely slowly. The lecture gives a natural clearance timescale of up to 70 years.

CCR5-Mutant Donor Case

p. 18

The lecture describes an HIV-infected man in Germany who developed acute myeloid leukemia and received a bone-marrow transplant in 2007. After immune ablation, he received donor cells homozygous for a CCR5 mutation that protects against HIV infection. He stopped antiretroviral therapy and remained without detectable HIV.

The lecture uses this case to motivate research aimed at eliminating or purging latently infected reservoirs.

Monocytes, Macrophages, and Lymphoid Organs

p. 18
  • Some monocyte subsets express CD4 and use CCR5 for HIV entry.
  • In the brain, monocytes and macrophages are major infected cell types and contribute to neuropsychiatric disease.
  • They are relatively resistant to HIV cytopathic effects, so they can persist as reservoirs and transport cells.
  • Infected monocytes can carry virus to organs such as the lungs and brain.
  • Lymph nodes contain most lymphocytes and provide an environment favorable to infection even during clinical latency.
  • Cytokines activate CD4 T cells, making them more susceptible to infection.
  • As disease advances, lymph-node architecture is destroyed and immune responsiveness deteriorates.

Clinical Findings Across Stages

p. 18-19
  • Acute HIV infection: fatigue, rash, headache, nausea, night sweats, and a mononucleosis-like syndrome.
  • Clinical latency: patient may look well for years while viral replication continues in lymphoid tissue.
  • Constitutional decline: weight loss, fever, night sweats, and progressive immune dysfunction.
  • The lecture describes a pre-AIDS prodrome of “diarrhea and dwindling” with fatigue, malaise, weight loss, fever, shortness of breath, chronic diarrhea, hairy leukoplakia, candidiasis, and lymphadenopathy.
  • AIDS: profound immunosuppression with severe opportunistic infections or unusual neoplasms, especially Kaposi sarcoma.

Plasma Viral Load vs CD4 Count

p. 19
Two major monitoring markers
MarkerBest use in the lectureKey interpretation
Plasma viral loadBest predictor of long-term outcome and treatment responseEach patient reaches a viral set point. A higher set point predicts faster progression and poorer treatment response.
CD4 countBetter predictor of short-term opportunistic infection riskAs CD4 falls, risk of opportunistic disease rises. The lecture uses <200 cells/µL as a major threshold.

Pediatric HIV

p. 19
  • Usually acquired from the mother during the perinatal period.
  • Infants commonly develop symptoms in less than 2 years. If untreated, death may follow within another 2 years.
  • Immature immunity makes neonates particularly vulnerable.
  • Lecture features include pneumonia, severe oral candidiasis, encephalopathy, stunting and wasting, lymphadenopathy, sepsis, hepatosplenomegaly, diarrhea, and growth retardation.
  • A high plasma viral load predicts rapid progression.

Neurologic Disease in HIV

p. 19
  • Lecture range: neurologic disease occurs in 40-90% of patients.
  • Syndromes include subacute encephalitis, vacuolar myelopathy, aseptic meningitis, and peripheral neuropathy.
  • AIDS dementia complex is the most common neurologic syndrome in the lecture and may affect up to 65% of AIDS patients.
  • Features: memory loss, poor concentration, apathy, and behavioral change.
  • Once severe dementia develops, average survival is <6 months.
  • Pediatric neurologic disease includes seizures, developmental delay, encephalopathy, and bacterial meningitis.

Opportunistic Infections

p. 19
  • Major cause of morbidity and mortality in late-stage HIV.
  • Common when CD4 < 200 cells/µL.
  • Protozoa: Toxoplasma gondii, Isospora, Cryptosporidium.
  • Fungi: Candida, Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, Pneumocystis jiroveci.
  • Bacteria: M. avium, M. tuberculosis, Listeria, Salmonella, Streptococcus species.
  • Viruses: CMV, HSV, VZV, JC virus, HBV, HCV.
  • Herpesviruses are especially frequent. The lecture calls CMV the most severe ocular complication.

Cancer in AIDS

p. 19
  • Kaposi sarcoma: associated with HHV-8.
  • Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: associated with EBV.
  • Cervical and anogenital cancers: associated with HPV.
  • With longer survival on ART, the lecture notes more Hodgkin lymphoma and liver, lung, and oral cancers.
  • Breast, colon, and prostate cancer risk is described as not increased.
  • Effective ART markedly reduced Kaposi sarcoma occurrence but had less effect on non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

HIV: Laboratory Diagnosis, Resistance Testing, Treatment, and Prevention

HIV testing combines serology with direct viral detection. The lecture then connects treatment to specific replication steps and stresses why combination therapy is necessary.

p. 19-21

Virus Isolation

p. 19
  • HIV can be cultured from peripheral-blood lymphocytes and occasionally other specimens.
  • Viral titers are generally higher in patients with AIDS than in asymptomatic infection.
  • The most sensitive isolation method is cocultivation with uninfected, mitogen-stimulated peripheral blood cells.
  • Growth is confirmed by detecting reverse transcriptase activity or virus-specific antigen such as p24.
  • Because isolation is slow and laborious, the lecture frames it as a research method.

Serology

p. 19
  • EIA or ELISA is the standard screening approach in the lecture, with sensitivity above 98%.
  • Historically, Western blot confirmation required any two bands among p24, gp41, or gp120/160.
  • The lecture notes that Western blot has been phased out by WHO and CDC and replaced by HIV RNA testing or newer fourth-generation assays.
  • Envelope antibodies remain detectable over time, while anti-p24 declines with progression.
  • Rapid antibody tests can use blood or oral fluid.
  • Mean seroconversion time is given as about 3-4 weeks, with nearly all patients positive within 6 months.

Nucleic Acid and Antigen Testing

p. 19-20
  • PCR enables early diagnosis by detecting HIV RNA before antibodies appear.
  • Viral load testing is the best correlate of disease stage and progression.
  • Nucleic acid methods listed: RT-PCR, DNA PCR, and branched DNA assays.
  • NAT is the gold standard for early infant diagnosis because maternal antibodies confound infant serology.
  • Plasma and whole blood are standard. Dried blood spots are useful in resource-limited settings.
  • p24 antigen appears before antibodies, then may disappear after antigen-antibody complex formation. Reappearance late in disease suggests a poor prognosis.
  • Fourth-generation assays combine HIV antibody and p24 antigen to shorten the window period.
  • Fifth-generation assays differentiate HIV-1 antibody, HIV-2 antibody, and p24 antigen.

Resistance and Tropism Testing

p. 20
  • Genotypic resistance testing: standard method. Sequences reverse transcriptase and protease genes for resistance mutations.
  • Interpretation uses expert resistance databases such as those maintained by the International AIDS Society and Stanford University.
  • Phenotypic testing: measures drug concentrations needed to inhibit viral replication. It is less common but helpful with complex resistance patterns.
  • Resistance testing is recommended at initial diagnosis and when treatment fails.
  • Additional assays may assess resistance to integrase or fusion inhibitors.
  • Coreceptor tropism testing helps predict response to CCR5 antagonist drugs.

Antiretroviral Drug Classes

p. 20
Antiviral classes in the lecture
Drug classAction
Reverse transcriptase inhibitorsBlock conversion of viral RNA into DNA.
Protease inhibitorsBlock essential viral proteases and prevent normal maturation of infectious particles.
Fusion inhibitorsPrevent viral entry.
Entry inhibitorsPrevent entry by blocking CCR5-dependent binding.
Integrase inhibitorsPrevent chromosomal integration of viral DNA.

Why Combination Therapy Matters

p. 20
  • Since 1996, HAART has used combinations that target multiple points in the HIV lifecycle.
  • Combination therapy can suppress viral replication to undetectable levels, allowing immune recovery and longer survival.
  • It does not cure HIV because latent reservoirs persist.
  • Monotherapy leads to rapid resistance.
  • Combination therapy delays resistance, although cross-resistance can occur.
  • Drug-resistant strains are increasingly recognized, including in newly diagnosed patients. The lecture notes about 19% resistant strains in perinatally infected infants.
  • Treatment is lifelong and can have adverse effects such as lipodystrophy. Access remains limited in some regions.

Antiretroviral Drugs as Prevention

p. 20
  • PrEP significantly lowers infection risk.
  • Zidovudine or AZT reduces mother-to-child transmission.
  • Shorter regimens using AZT or nevirapine have been used in resource-limited settings.
  • Breastfeeding transmission remains a challenge in the lecture discussion.

Why an HIV Vaccine Is Difficult

p. 20-21
  • No candidate vaccine has been fully effective in the lecture.
  • HIV mutates rapidly.
  • The virus is not expressed in every infected cell.
  • The host does not completely eliminate HIV after primary infection.
  • The exact correlates of protective immunity are not established.
  • The lecture notes a shortage of ideal animal models. Chimpanzees develop viremia and antibodies but not immunodeficiency. The SIV-macaque model develops simian AIDS and is useful in vaccine studies.
  • Research approaches named include recombinant envelope glycoproteins, viral vectors, and gene-therapy strategies aimed at making cells resistant to HIV.

Patient Education

p. 21
  • Adherence to antiretroviral therapy is essential.
  • Regular monitoring includes viral load and CD4 testing.
  • Transmission prevention includes safe sex, avoiding needle sharing, and responsible disclosure.
  • The lecture encourages balanced diet, exercise, and mental-health support.
  • Vaccination and prophylaxis reduce the burden of opportunistic infections.
  • Counseling, peer support, and stigma reduction are part of comprehensive care.

Cram Sheet

Fast recall of the lecture's must-know distinctions, mechanisms, values, and diagnostic or preventive anchors.

Rabies in One Chainp. 4
Bite or scratch → local persistence → nicotinic acetylcholine receptor interaction in muscle → retrograde fast axonal transport → CNS spread → centrifugal spread → salivary gland replication and shedding.

Rabies Must-Knows

p. 1-6
  • Rhabdoviridae, Lyssavirus. Bullet-shaped, enveloped, non-segmented negative-sense ssRNA.
  • Genome order: 3′ Leader → N → P → M → G → L → Trailer 5′.
  • N mRNA most abundant. L mRNA least abundant. Cause: transcription attenuation.
  • Accumulating N protein switches polymerase behavior from separate mRNA transcription to full-length genome replication.
  • Negri body = pathognomonic eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion in Purkinje cells and hippocampal pyramidal neurons. Not present in every case.
  • Furious ~80%: hydrophobia, aerophobia, hyperexcitability, autonomic dysfunction.
  • Paralytic ~20%: flaccid weakness, no hydrophobia, may mimic Guillain-Barré syndrome.
  • No pre-symptomatic diagnostic test is described in the lecture.
  • Category I: no vaccine, no RIG.
  • Category II: vaccine, no RIG.
  • Category III: vaccine + RIG.
  • Category II on head or neck → manage as Category III.

Slow Infection and Prion Must-Knows

p. 6-7
  • SSPE: chronic nonpermissive measles infection. Early measles → 6-8 years latency → progressive neurologic decline. CSF anti-measles antibody is elevated.
  • PML: JC virus reactivation in immunosuppression → multifocal demyelination. Diagnose with CSF JCV PCR plus MRI pattern.
  • Prions: protein only. No RNA or DNA.
  • PrPSc converts PrPC to the abnormal conformation.
  • No inflammatory or immune response. No treatment. Fatal in the lecture.
  • Kuru: ritual cannibalism. CJD: dementia + ataxia + myoclonus.

Viral Carcinogenesis Must-Knows

p. 7-14
  • About 15-20% of human tumors have a viral cause in the lecture.
  • Viral cancer is usually a multistep process. Infection alone is often not sufficient.
  • Core molecular pattern: oncogene activation + tumor-suppressor loss.
  • p53: DNA-damage checkpoint and apoptosis. Rb: cell-cycle brake before S phase.
  • HPV E6 → p53. HPV E7 → Rb.
  • SV40 large T → p53 + Rb.
  • EBV LMP1 → TRAF-linked NF-κB and MAPK activation.
  • HBV → HCC. X protein plus chronic injury. Aflatoxin increases risk.
  • HCV → HCC through chronic inflammation and cirrhosis.
  • HTLV → adult T-cell leukemia or lymphoma. TAX dysregulates gene expression.
  • HIV cancers are indirect because HIV causes immune suppression rather than direct cellular transformation.

HPV Must-Knows

p. 13-14
  • Low-risk: 6, 11 → anogenital warts and laryngeal papillomas.
  • High-risk: 16, 18 strongest association with cervical cancer. 31, 33, 45, 56 are moderate-risk types in the lecture.
  • Benign or premalignant lesions: HPV DNA usually episomal.
  • Cancer: persistent high-risk infection with integrated viral DNA is a key pattern.
  • Most infections clear within 2-3 years.
  • Bivalent: 16, 18. Quadrivalent: 6, 11, 16, 18. 9-valent: 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58.
  • HPV vaccine is preventive, not therapeutic.
HIV Entry in One Linep. 16
gp120 binds CD4 → CCR5 or CXCR4 coreceptor engagement → gp41 triggers membrane fusion.
CCR5 = macrophage-tropic.
CXCR4 = lymphocyte-tropic.

HIV Genes You Need to Recognize

p. 15
Compact HIV gene map
GeneFast recall
gagCore proteins
proProtease
polReverse transcriptase and other replication enzymes
envEnvelope glycoproteins gp120 and gp41
Tat↑ viral transcription
RevExports unspliced RNA
Nef↓ CD4 and MHC I, ↑ infectivity

VifBlocks APOBEC3G

HIV Progression Anchors

p. 17-19
  • 4-11 days: mucosal infection to initial viremia.
  • 8-12 weeks: viremia and dissemination window.
  • 3-6 weeks: 50-75% develop acute mononucleosis-like illness.
  • 1-3 months: immune response lowers viremia and partially restores CD4 count.
  • ~10 years: typical clinical-latency period in untreated infection.
  • Clinical latency still has intense viral activity, including about 10 billion particles produced and destroyed daily.
  • Memory CD4 cells and monocytes or macrophages sustain persistent reservoirs.
  • CD4 <200 cells/µL → major opportunistic-infection risk.

HIV Diagnosis and Monitoring

p. 19-20
  • EIA or ELISA: screening.
  • NAT or RT-PCR: detects HIV before antibody and measures viral load.
  • NAT = gold standard for early infant diagnosis.
  • p24: early antigen. May fall after seroconversion and reappear late with poor prognosis.
  • 4th gen: antibody + p24.
  • 5th gen: differentiates HIV-1 Ab, HIV-2 Ab, and p24.
  • Viral load: best long-term predictor and treatment monitor.
  • CD4 count: best short-term predictor of opportunistic-infection risk.

Treatment and Prevention Anchors

p. 20-21
  • RT inhibitors: block RNA → DNA.
  • Integrase inhibitors: block chromosomal integration.
  • Protease inhibitors: block maturation.
  • Fusion and entry inhibitors: block entry.
  • HAART uses combination therapy. Monotherapy rapidly selects resistance.
  • ART suppresses replication but does not eradicate latent reservoirs.
  • PrEP lowers acquisition risk.
  • AZT reduces mother-to-child transmission.
  • Vaccine development is difficult because of rapid mutation, incomplete viral expression in infected cells, persistent infection, uncertain correlates of protection, and limited animal models.
Final Exam Trapsp. 6-20
Prion = no nucleic acid.
HIV = not directly oncogenic.
Clinical latency ≠ absence of replication.
Viral load predicts long-term outcome. CD4 predicts near-term opportunistic infection risk.
HPV vaccine prevents targeted infection but does not treat established disease.
Rabies Category II on the head or neck is managed as Category III.
